Q. Huang,a,b,∗,z T. W. Lyons,a and W. D. Sidesa,∗∗
<sup>a</sup>Department ofChemical and Biological Engineering, The University ofAlabama, Tuscaloosa, Alabama 35487, USA

The effect of dimethylglyoxime on Co electrodeposition was investigated with cyclic voltammetry, chronopotentiometry, quartz
microbalance as well as electrochemical impedance. A potential dependent suppression effect was observed at low potential with
a breakdown of the suppression at high potential, resulting in a hysteresis in CV. The addition of dimethylglyoxime not only
causes a fast and strong suppression in potential transients but also modifies the impedance spectra. Additional capacitive loops
and inductance loops emerged depending on the applied potential, suggesting a competitive adsorption between different surface
adsorbed intermediates. A relaxation of suppression effect was observed in absence of agitation and a strong suppression was
re-established upon agitation. A reverse relation between Co deposition rate and rotation rate was observed when the rotation rate is
below a critical value, providing a path to enable the preferential deposition at the bottom of a small damascene feature.

The state-of-the-art back-end-of-line (BEOL) interconnects are
fabricated with copper, which replaced Aluminum in late 1990’s due
to its lower resistivity and superior reliability.<sup>1,2</sup> As the interconnect
continues to scale, the critical dimension of the BEOL structures has
approached the electron mean free path of copper. The copper resis-
tivity in such nanostructures increases exponentially as the dimension
further shrinks,<sup>3,4</sup> posing tremendous challenges to the continuous
scaling of copper interconnect for 7 nm technology and beyond. While
the bulk resistivity of a metal is an intrinsic property of the material
its resistivity in these small structures is largely determined by what
happens to the electrons when they come across an interface, i.e., the
surface of the metal structure in contact with the matrix materials,
the boundaries between grains in the metal structure and the internal
interface between metal and the embedded impurity species.<sup>5</sup> Metals
with shorter electron mean free path are less susceptible to the effect
of scaling and may appear advantageous for the interconnect appli-
cation. For example, transition metals including Ni, Co, Mo and Ru
were predicted to be potential candidates to replace Cu.<sup>6</sup>
In addition to the advantage of a shorter mean free path, some
of the candidate metals can potentially provide performance gain
through innovative integration schemes. The overall resistance of an
interconnect structure is a result of not only the copper but also other
materials used in the interconnect structure for a variety of purposes.
Such materials include diffusion barrier, adhesion layer, capping layer
and sometimes additional elements as the seed layer for copper plating.
Therefore, using metals that can serve dual or multiple purposes may
allow more volume for the conducting metal and thus a lower overall
resistance and an improved RC delay. Furthermore, new materials
that enable better integration and lower defectivities can improve the
overall performance as well. For example, chemical vapor deposited
(CVD) and atomic layer deposited (ALD) Ru was previously studied
to replace the Ta diffusion barrier – Cu seed stack.<sup>7–9</sup>
Co has recently gained more and more attention as a material to
replace the traditional Ta liner.<sup>10,11</sup> Compared with Ta, Co provides a
better wettability of PVD Cu seed, enables a more conformal Cu seed
coverage and therefore improves the extendibility of Cu electroplat-
ing in smaller dimensions.<sup>12</sup> In addition, the enhanced grain growth
of Cu electroplated on Co seed<sup>13</sup> and the self-formation of a barrier
layer enabled by the Mn diffusion through Co layer<sup>14</sup> potentially pro-
vide additional performance gain on the reliability of the interconnect
structures.
Recently, selectively electroless deposited Co has been demon-
strated to partially or completely replace the Cu in the small vias to
improve the via resistance.<sup>15</sup> The bottom up fill of the via structures re-
lied on the selectivity between the exposed underneath metal layer and
the dielectrics for electroless deposition process. Electrolytic super
conformal deposition of Co and Ni was reported using 2-mercapto-
5-benzimidazolesulfonic acid (MBIS).<sup>16–19</sup> A potential dependent ad-
sorption, passivation and desorption of the additive was found to
result in a negative differential resistance in cyclic voltammetry and
therefore multiple steady states at certain potentials. Super conformal
deposition of through silicon vias (TSV) was enabled by controlling
the deposition at such potentials, where the bottom and top of a TSV
are plated at two different states. Super conformal NiFe filling into
sub-50 nm interconnect trenches was demonstrated with a two com-
ponent additive system using a polymer suppressor and a monomer
accelerator.<sup>20</sup> More recently, three component commercial additive
has been reported for the bottom up filling of Co for interconnect.<sup>21</sup>
Electrodeposition of cobalt and its alloys has been studied ex-
tensively in the past for their magnetic properties. Among them,
CoNiFe<sup>22–25</sup> and CoFe<sup>26–28</sup> alloys were used in commercial hard disk
drive writing heads for their low coercivities and high moments. The
two additives commonly used in magnetic thin film plating, saccha-
rin and thiourea, were studied with scanning tunneling microscope
and were found to adsorb on Au(111) surface through physisorption
and chemisorption respectively.<sup>29</sup> The different sulfur incorporation
behaviors resulted in different coercivities of the deposited films.
A group of additives including saccharin and thiourea were previ-
ously studied for their impacts on the NiFe alloy deposition toward
superconformal filling.<sup>20</sup> While polyethyleneimine (PEI) was found
to show suppression effect, thiourea and benzenesulfinic acid showed
only acceleration effect. In addition, mercapto-benezenimidazole and
its sulfonic acid derivative showed suppression followed by acceler-
ation effect. Comparing the molecular structures of these additives
in Figure 1, it is clear that PEI only has paired amine groups, which
are two CH groups apart. Thiourea and benzenesulfinic acid both
have mercapto groups vie an isomerization and a disproportionation
reaction,<sup>30</sup> respectively. When both mercapto group and paired amine
(or imine) groups are present in the molecules, such as mercapto-
benezenimidazole and its sulfonic acid derivative, both suppression
and acceleration effects were observed. In addition, when one of the
paired amine nitrogen is replaced by oxygen in mercapto-benzoxazole,
the suppression effect was significantly weakened and only accel-
eration effect was observed. Finally, when the mercapto group was
removed and only a sulfonic group is present in saccharin, neither sup-
pression nor acceleration was observed. Based on this previous work,

the effect of dimethylglyoxime (DMG) on the electrodeposition of
cobalt. DMG and other dioxime have been previously used as an

The effect of DMG on Co deposition was studied with cyclic
voltammetry (CV). A layer of Co was pre-plated on Pt RDE using
the makeup electrolyte (DMG free). Potential was scanned from open
circuit potential (OCP, typically about 0.48 V SCE) to 1.5 V with

of 10 mA/cm<sup>2</sup> in the HCl stripping solution using a rotation rate of
900 rpm. A sudden potential increase was observed once the Co film
was completely stripped. The total charge before the potential increase
was used to calculate the amount of Co deposited.
Potential transient studies during galvanostatic plating with injec-
tion of DMG were also conducted using Pt RDE rotating at 100 rpm.
In these studies, small amount of DMG concentrate was injected at
the vicinity of the cathode with the potential transients recorded. Gold
quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) preplated with Co from a DMG
free solution was used to study the current transients at fixed potentials
in absence of agitation. Because of the tiny solution volume used in
QCM Co electrolyte with double concentration of the desired DMG
concentration was used in the injection of DMG. For example, 2 ml
of Co solution with 200 ppm DMG was added into 2 ml DMG free
Co solution in QCM cell to obtain the injection of 100 ppm DMG.
The same chronoamperometry measurements were also carried out
on pre-plated Pt RDE with changes in rotation rates. Electrochemical
impedance spectra were acquired using Co pre-plated Pt RDE at 100
rpm. All electrochemical studies were conducted using an AutoLab
electrochemical station with QCM and frequency analyzer modules.
Results and Discussion
The effect of DMG on Co deposition was first examined with cyclic
voltammetry (CV). A 100 nm layer of cobalt was deposited on Pt disc
electrode in the additive free solution before each CV. A change of
open circuit potential (OCP) from about 0.3 V to 0.48 V (both vs.
SCE) was observed before and after this pre-plating. Potential was
then swept from 0.48 V to 1.5 V with a sweep rate of 5 mV/sec.
Figure 2 shows the CV curves with different amounts of DMG without
and with ohmic drop correction. When no DMG was present in the
solution, the cathodic deposition current started at 0.7 V and reached
a current density of 2 mA/cm<sup>2</sup> at 0.8 V and 4 mA/cm<sup>2</sup> at 0.85 V.
The forward and backward scans coincided with each other. The
addition of 10 ppm DMG did not change the CV behavior. However,
when 100 ppm DMG was added into the solution, the deposition
was significantly polarized at low current range. The onset of the
cathodic reaction did not occur until 0.9 V, after which a sudden
jump of the cathodic reaction rate was observed. Furthermore, the
suppressed cathodic current at low potential was not observed in the
backward scan, resulting in a hysteresis in CV. Further increase of
DMG concentration to 300 ppm resulted in stronger suppression of
the cathodic current. This suppression was present regardless of the
potential, causing a much diminished hysteresis. Figure 2b presents
the same CV curves with the ohmic resistance of solution accounted
for using impedance measurement. The sudden current increase in
the case of 100 ppm DMG was so significant that the CV showed a
S-shaped negative differential resistance after the ohmic correction.
